stories.headline: Why stubble fires keep coming back
stories.deck: Stubble burning is the result of a combination of legal, technological and economic factors, including the paddy-wheat cycle, assured procurement and a narrow window between crops; a lasting solution needs stronger incentives for diversification, better residue management and more reliable measurement of burning
stories.bodyText:
It is that time of the year when air pollution in North India, and in Delhi in particular, takes centre stage in public discourse. One oft-cited reason for the worsening air quality index (AQI) is stubble burning by farmers.
Why farmers burn stubble
Stubble burning is the practice of setting fire to crop residue, consisting of the lower parts of plants left after harvesting. This practice is prevalent from the beginning of October to the end of November across northwest India, especially in Punjab, Haryana, and parts of Uttar Pradesh. Stubble burning is mainly associated with the burning of paddy straw in Punjab and Haryana, which together produce around 29 million metric tons of paddy straw. Stubble burning releases large amounts of particulate matter, carbon monoxide, volatile organic compounds (VOCs), and other carcinogenic substances, which together form a thick smog that can harm human health. It also leads to a loss of soil fertility by depleting nitrogen, sulphur, potash, phosphorus, and other micronutrients. The heat generated by stubble burning results in a loss of soil moisture and organic content, which, in turn, leads to increased use of fertilizers in the next crop cycle.
Stubble burning is not a new phenomenon. It has been practised in Punjab since the late 1970s and early 1980s, largely following the introduction of combine harvesters, which leave a portion of the plant in the soil after harvesting. What has changed is its timing, which now coincides with the winter months in North India. This shift in timing followed the enactment of the Punjab Preservation of Sub-Soil Water Act, 2009 (PPSSWA 2009).
In 2012, nearly 73% of the cropped area in Punjab was irrigated using groundwater resources. There was a deficit of 14.31 billion cubic metres, which was met through excessive withdrawal of groundwater. Groundwater levels in Punjab declined at an alarming rate of 0.36 metres annually between 1999 and 2009, driven by intense over-exploitation for agriculture. A landmark NASA GRACE satellite study in 2009 showed that the region comprising Punjab, Haryana and Rajasthan lost 109 cubic kilometres of groundwater between 2002 and 2008 alone, which was considered the largest instance of groundwater depletion in the world at the time.
Water crisis
The PPSSWA 2009 was a result of this alarming situation. The main goal of the Act was to prevent rapid groundwater depletion by prohibiting early paddy nursery sowing and transplantation before the arrival of the monsoon rains. The Act prohibited farmers from sowing paddy before May 10 and transplanting it before June 10, thus delaying paddy transplantation to align with the monsoon season. To ensure compliance, the Act prescribed stringent punishments. Implementing officers were authorised to destroy paddy sown in contravention of the Act and impose a penalty of ₹10,000 per hectare for every month of contravention. These actions by officials were also exempt from legal scrutiny
These sowing restrictions under PPSSWA 2009 pushed the paddy harvest to late October and early November, leaving farmers a narrow 10-15-day window to prepare their fields for the next wheat crop and reducing the time available for sowing. The PUSA-44 variety, which produces higher yields but takes 150-160 days to harvest, further narrowed the window between paddy harvesting and wheat sowing. Combine harvesters, which leave about a foot of stubble behind, put heavy pressure on farmers to clear the crop residue in a very short time. Manual clearing is time-consuming and expensive. Together, these factors made stubble burning almost a necessity for farmers.
The moot point is why farmers continue to grow paddy and wheat despite a stringent legal framework and depleting groundwater levels. The answer lies in the incentive structure built for these two crops. The present minimum support price and procurement framework heavily favours rice and wheat procurement in Punjab and Haryana. Between 2012 and 2024, average paddy procurement in India was about 37% of production. The corresponding figures for Punjab and Haryana were 87% and 74%, respectively, more than double the national average. The pattern is similar for wheat, with procurement accounting for 30% of production nationally, compared with 70% in Punjab and 63% in Haryana. It needs to be noted that the computation of national averages includes Punjab and Haryana, and if these two States are excluded, the differences could be even higher. Such a system provides assured incomes to producers of these two crops in these two States, discouraging them from diversifying into other crops. In addition, power is free for farmers in Punjab and almost free in Haryana. This further encourages farmers to grow water-intensive crops like paddy and wheat through groundwater extraction.
Incentive problem
The technical solutions to stubble burning fall broadly into two categories: in-situ measures that include the use of crop residue management (CRM) machines such as Happy Seeders, Super Seeders and Rotavators; short-duration rice varieties; and direct seeding of rice; and ex-situ measures that involve using crop residue for alternative energy production, such as bio-ethanol and compressed biogas. However, both approaches face formidable problems. Happy Seeders and Super Seeders require an expensive 60-horsepower (HP) tractor, which remains unused for most of the year. Even hiring one typically costs a farmer ₹10,000 and involves a long waiting period. Ex-situ measures cost ₹1,500-₹2,500 per acre, a significant expense for many farmers.
The economic approach to address stubble burning involves building an incentive structure for farmers to diversify from paddy to other crops. The National Green Tribunal ruled in 2018 that farmers who burn stubble could be excluded from the purview of the minimum support price (MSP) policy. The Supreme Court upheld this view in 2023. During the stubble burning season of 2025, 31 flying squads by CPCB were deployed in 18 districts of Punjab and 13 districts of Haryana, involving 10,500 field functionaries in Punjab and 10,000 in Haryana.
Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) has directed that complaints be filed before the judiciary against the officials responsible for the lack of effective monitoring. The Parliamentary Committee on air quality, however, advocated that penalising farmers should be the last resort. The Committee recommended setting a minimum price covering all the costs for selling stubble for ex-situ measures, which can ensure farmers’ guaranteed income.
The government of Punjab mostly adopted in-situ CRM-based measures and limited ex-situ initiatives. CAQM observed in 2025 that a lot is required to be done in Punjab in terms of timely availability of CRM machinery, necessary support for CBG plants and other industries utilizing paddy straw, and better enforcement. On the other hand, Haryana adopted an incentive-based approach, along the lines of the Parliamentary Panel’s recommendations, in addition to in-situ and ex-situ measures. A financial incentive of ₹1,000/acre for CRM use; ₹4,000/acre for direct seeding of rice; ₹7,000/acre for diversification to alternate crops; and incentives to panchayats for better performance have been put in place.
Punjab and Haryana are reported to have collectively achieved a 90% reduction in stubble burning incidents during paddy harvesting in 2025 in comparison to the same period in 2022 (Lok Sabha starred question No. 18, 1.12.2025). However, this assessment needs to be interpreted with caution, given some issues in measurement.
Measurement problem
Presently, the CREAMS (Consortium for Research on Agroecosystem Monitoring and Modeling from Space) protocol used for measuring stubble burning is built on NASA’s MODIS and VIIRS satellites. These are polar satellites that orbit the earth’s poles and observe India only at fixed times of the day, from 10:30 am to 1:30 pm. Their sensors are able to capture only active fires and are unable to compute the actual number of fires over a 24-hour period. According to a report by the International Forum for Environment, Sustainability and Technology in 2025, when data from multiple satellites was used to compute the actual land area affected by fire, the reduction was more gradual, at around 30%. A Current Science study in November 2025, led by scientists from ISRO using geostationary satellite observations, showed that farmers have shifted to stubble burning in the evening hours to avoid polar satellites. This study suggested using both polar and geostationary satellite data for an accurate picture of stubble burning.
Conclusion
In conclusion, stubble burning is a complex phenomenon driven by technological, economic and legal factors. The solution should be a judicious mix of the short-term in-situ and ex-situ measures with the medium/long term crop diversification (away from paddy). There needs to be an improvement in the methodology of measurement. Penal provisions are unlikely to be useful as there can be perverse incentives for collusion between farmers and officials, which may lead to ‘showing’ a reduction, rather than an actual reduction.
(C.S.C.Sekhar is professor of economics, Institute of Economic Growth, Delhi University)

stories.headline: Counting begins for Bengal bypolls, BJP's first electoral test after coming to power
stories.deck: The counting started amid tight security arrangements at the designated centres in both constituencies, with officials first taking up postal ballots and Electronically Transmitted Postal Ballots before proceeding with the EVM votes.
stories.bodyText:
Counting of votes began at 8 a.m. on Friday (October 9, 2026) for the Nandigram and Rejinagar Assembly bypolls, the first electoral test for the BJP since it came to power in West Bengal in May this year.
The counting started amid tight security arrangements at the designated centres in both constituencies, with officials first taking up postal ballots and Electronically Transmitted Postal Ballots (ETPB) before proceeding with the EVM votes.
The counting at both seats is taking place in two halls and is scheduled to be completed in 15 rounds, with separate halls earmarked for postal ballots and ETPB votes.
The results will not have any impact on the government, as the BJP has won 207 seats out of the total of 294.
The two constituencies witnessed a high turnout of around 80% on Tuesday (October 6, 2026), with Nandigram recording 80.89% polling and Rejinagar 80.08%.
The Election Commission had described Tuesday's (October 6, 2026) polling as "more or less peaceful".
Opposition parties, however, alleged voter intimidation, booth-level irregularities and the removal of their polling agents from booths and demanded fresh polling.
The BJP rejected the allegations and maintained that the polling was peaceful.
The arrest of Aam Janata Unnayan Party chief Humayun Kabir following a confrontation with police in Rejinagar was among the major flashpoints during the polling.
The by-election was required as Mr. Kabir vacated the seat and retained Nowda.
The results are being keenly watched for the BJP's performance after replacing the 15-year-old Trinamool Congress regime as the ruling party following the 2026 Assembly elections, as well as the shape of the opposition space amid a split in the TMC and the presence of multiple political formations.
In Nandigram, Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari had defeated TMC supremo Mamata Banerjee in 2021 and won the seat again in the 2026 Assembly polls before retaining Bhabanipur, necessitating the bypoll.
The BJP has fielded Hasirani Rath, while Congress nominee Milan Pradhan is backed by the Mamata Banerjee-led TMC faction after its candidate withdrew. A rival TMC faction led by Ritabrata Banerjee is also in the fray.
In Rejinagar, the contest is between BJP's Sakharav Sarkar, Mamata-led TMC candidate Rabiul Alam Chowdhury, rival TMC nominee Safiuzzaman Sheikh, Congress' Mohammad Abdullahil Kafi, CPI(M)'s Syed Asad Ali and AJUP candidate Golam Nabi Azad, son of party chief Humayun Kabir.

stories.headline: US lawmaker Krishnamoorthi honours Indian pilot Smit Machchhar
stories.bodyText: Washington: US Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi on Friday honoured Indian pilot Smit Machchhar for his extraordinary bravery aboard the flydubai flight that saved 172 lives. . Captain Machchhar was attacked by his co-pilot and seriously injured in the cockpit of flydubai flight FZ1073 on September 30 while it was travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv. . Despite being severely injured, Captain Machchhar opened the cockpit door, enabling passengers to overpower the attacker. . Krishnamoorthi, the Democratic Congressman from Illinois, has submitted a statement for the US Congressional Record. . “After being attacked by the flight’s first officer, who attempted to seize control of the aircraft, Captain Machchhar’s actions helped save the lives of 172 passengers and his fellow crew members,” Krishnamoorthi said. . He noted that there were four US citizens and 27 children among the 172 passengers on board the Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv. . “... I rise today to recognise Captain Smit Machchhar of India, a husband, father, and pilot with 17 years of flying experience, including 11 as a captain, whose extraordinary bravery on September 30, 2026, helped save the lives of 172 passengers and his fellow crew members aboard Flydubai Flight 1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv, including four United States citizens and 27 children,” Krishnamoorthi said. . He said when the first officer attacked Captain Machchhar, the aircraft plunged approximately 16,000 feet in about 30 seconds. . “Despite grave injuries, Captain Machchhar fought his way to the cockpit door and opened it, allowing passengers and crew members to enter and overpower his attacker. Two reserve Flydubai pilots travelling aboard the aircraft then took control and landed it safely in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia,” Krishnamoorthi said. .Mumbaikars hail hero pilot Smit Machchhar who saved 174 lives on flydubai flight. He said even as Captain Machchhar fought for his own life, he understood that the lives of everyone aboard depended on what he did next. . “Despite his injuries, his years of experience told him that the aircraft was going down, and he found the strength to reach that door. His presence of mind, determination, and courage gave the passengers and crew the chance they needed to stop the attack and avert a catastrophe,” Krishnamoorthi said. . Behind every person aboard Flight 1073 is a family that was spared an unimaginable loss. Because Captain Machchhar refused to give up, the passengers and crew aboard that aircraft had the chance to return to the people who love them. . “... I ask my colleagues to join me in honouring Captain Smit Machchhar, whose extraordinary courage helped save hundreds of lives aboard Flight 1073. We extend our warmest wishes to him, his wife Sonal, their two children, and their entire family, and we hope for the captain’s full-speed recovery from his injuries at the earliest,” Krishnamoorthi said.

stories.headline: Environment protection versus strategic infrastructure: SC seeks Punjab plan on afforestation
stories.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: In what appeared to be a clash between environment protection and strategic infrastructure in a border state, the Supreme Court on Thursday asked Punjab govt its plan on allocation of land for compensatory afforestation in lieu of tree felling necessitated for construction of highway and public projects in the state.
Solicitor general Tushar Mehta told a bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana that the Punjab and Haryana HC has imposed a blanket bank on tree felling without the HC’s prior permission which had brought to a standstill that strategic road projects in the border state even though necessary permission for these had been obtained from statutory authorities.
The bench said the HC’s concern was legitimate as the forest cover in Punjab has been reduced to 3.67% of the geographical area, which is lesser than the 4.87% forest cover in the arid Rajasthan. Compensatory afforestation would be the best possible answer, the bench said.
SG said that for that land must be made available by the state. The bench asked the state govt to file a detailed proposal on provisioning land for compensatory afforestation whenever trees are required to be felled for highway projects.

The HC, while imposing a blanket ban on tree felling, had flagged the poor forest cover in the state and said, “It appears that the functionaries of the state of Punjab are neither serious nor they seem conscious of the impending ecological catastrophe. 
In view of the inactivity of the respondents, it requires drastic remedial measures by this court. Accordingly, this court prohibits the cutting of any tree of any age/species in Punjab, without permission of this Court, till the next date of hearing.”
In another case, the HC had said trees would be permitted to be cut if the state makes available and allots public land for the purpose of compensatory afforestation (planting of five times the number of trees cut) within a radius of five km of the place where the trees are felled. It had said that if the state failed to provide such land, then the cutting of trees would not take place.
Mehta said that in linear highway projects, there may not be suitable land within five km of the project for afforestation and requested the court to relax this norm to enable afforestation at the nearest possible location.

stories.headline: MIT-WPU research detects microplastics in freshwater fish consumed in Pune
stories.bodyText: Mumbai: Plastic pollution is no longer limited to marine ecosystems. An ongoing doctoral study at Pune-based MIT World Peace University (MIT-WPU) has detected microplastics in freshwater fish commonly consumed in the city, highlighting the need for greater understanding of how plastic pollution moves through freshwater ecosystems and enters the food chain. The research focuses on commercially consumed freshwater fish, particularly Rohu and Tilapia, to examine the occurrence, characteristics and potential sources of microplastic contamination, as well as its implications for freshwater ecosystems and human health. The research is being conducted by Simran Singh, PhD Scholar, Department of Environmental Studies, MIT-WPU, under the guidance of Dr. Soma Mishra. . The study is funded through the MIT World Peace University Seed Grant. The research began with a detailed mapping of Pune’s freshwater fish supply chain. Rather than focusing only on retail markets, the researchers surveyed major wholesalers and distributors, which serve as key entry points for freshwater fish into the city. Pune was divided into four geographical zones for the survey, covering the city’s major distribution networks. The researchers interviewed 26 wholesalers and distributors across Pune. Based on the survey, the study estimates that approximately 37–40 tonnes of freshwater fish enter the Pune market every day, with Rohu and Tilapia among the commonly traded species. A significant proportion of the supply comes from aquaculture systems, while fish are also transported to Pune from states and regions including Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat, Ratnagiri, Mumbai and Kolkata, reflecting the extensive interstate nature of the city’s freshwater fish supply chain. The laboratory investigation detected microplastics in the freshwater fish samples examined. The particles identified included fibres, fragments and pellets, which are among the commonly reported forms of microplastics found in freshwater environments. Based on the detected levels and local consumption patterns, the study estimates that an individual consuming an average of 250 grams of freshwater fish twice a week over 50 years could potentially ingest between 93,600 and 124,800 microplastic particles. “Most discussions on microplastic pollution focus on marine environments. However, freshwater ecosystems and inland cities like Pune remain relatively understudied, despite being important sources of fish consumed by local communities. Our objective was to understand the complete journey of fish before it reaches consumers. Instead of surveying small retail markets, we focused on wholesalers and distributors because they represent the primary entry points of freshwater fish into Pune,” said Singh. The study aims to establish baseline scientific data on freshwater microplastic pollution in Pune, a rapidly urbanising city, and contribute to a better understanding of the pathways through which microplastics may move from freshwater environments into the food chain. The findings could support evidence-based approaches to plastic waste management, wastewater management, freshwater ecosystem conservation and food safety.

briefs.headline: TCS sees no impact from U.S. green card programme suspension on workforce strategy
briefs.deck: Stating an earlier announcement, the IT firm said that it intends to hire an additional 15,000 people in the U.S. over the next five years, “to further augment local workforce”
briefs.bodyText:
Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), India’s top IT services exporter, said on Friday (October 9, 2026) that it does not expect the U.S. suspension of the Permanent Labour Certification (PERM) programme for IT companies to have any material impact on its workforce strategy or client engagements.
The statement comes after the U.S. on Thursday (October 8, 2026) suspended IT firms, including Tata, from the PERM programme, which allows companies to apply for green cards for H-1B visa workers. The other companies named were Cognizant, Infosys, Wipro, HCL, Capgemini, Microsoft and Adobe.
“Our PERM applications were in single digits in the last two years and hence we do not expect the suspension of the program to impact our workforce strategy and customer engagements,” TCS said in its statement.
Stating an earlier announcement, the firm said that it intends to hire an additional 15,000 people in the U.S. over the next five years, “to further augment local workforce”.
“Our workforce strategy in the US is anchored in hiring local talent, supported by a robust campus recruitment model. We have built a significant local workforce across 31 offices and delivery centers throughout the country,” the statement read.

briefs.headline: Untying the knot in Telangana, one childhood at a time
briefs.deck: Despite a steady decline in child marriages in Telangana, the practice continues. Poverty, social pressures and family circumstances continue to place girls at risk of being married early, with consequences for their education, health and independence. Abhinay Deshpande examines the persisting issue and its impact on young lives
briefs.bodyText:
Last December, 15-year-old Tanya* dressed for what she thought would be a temple visit. Her aunt helped her wear a langa voni, the traditional half-saree. Tanya was looking forward to the outing. But the temple visit was only what she had been told; her family was actually preparing for a prospective groom to come and see her, with marriage already being discussed.
A Class VI dropout, Tanya hails from a tribal hamlet in Nizamabad district of Telangana. She is the only child of her mother, who worked as a labourer before health problems forced her to stop. Her estranged father, who has tuberculosis and is unable to work, lives with his first wife and their children.

briefs.headline: Vaibhav Sooryavanshi’s presence puts Sanju Samson under pressure
briefs.deck: Ishan Kishan is returning to his hometown of Ranchi, ready to take on the West Indies in the second T20I. This match offers a golden opportunity for Kishan to demonstrate his skill and confidence. The batting coach of India highlighted their unwavering fearless attitude towards the game. With selection decisions on bowlers and batting spots pending, players are eager to impress.
briefs.bodyText:
Ranchi: Nearly four years after his last international appearance at the JSCA International Cricket Stadium, 
Ishan Kishan
 returns to familiar territory on Friday when India take on the West Indies in the second T20I, carrying the form and confidence of a player who has fought his way back into the Indian team.
Ishan’s last international game here came in January 2023, when India lost a T20I to New Zealand. Much has changed since then. He subsequently lost his place in the India set-up, was dropped from the BCCI central contract list and then embarked on a comeback that has eventually seen him become an integral part of the national side.
Now, with good form behind him and his home crowd in front of him, Ishan has a chance to turn his long-awaited return to Ranchi into a memorable one. He will be keen to make his own contribution as India look to take a 2-0 lead in the series.
India batting coach Sitanshu Kotak said the change of venue would not alter the team’s philosophy.
“The way we are approaching the game, with a fearless approach and putting the team first, that’s the same way we will go,” Kotak said ahead of the game here on Thursday.
Yet, Ranchi could demand a little more adaptability than the opening game did.
Though Kotak said “the pitch looked a good batting track” on the eve of the match, the venue has not traditionally been a high-scoring T20 ground. In the four T20Is played here, the 200-run mark has never been breached, with India’s 196/6 against Sri Lanka in 2016 remaining the highest score. New Zealand have also successfully defended 176 at the venue.
Rain and cool, cloudy conditions could add another variable, while dew may become important later in the evening. With temperatures expected to hover between 22°C and 24°C during match time, India could have to balance their attack carefully, particularly if they end up bowling second.
That brings another selection question. Mayank Yadav was expensive in the opening game, leaving India to consider whether to persist with the express quick or bring fit-again Prince Yadav into the attack. They also have considerable spin depth, with Axar Patel, Kuldeep Yadav, Ravi Bishnoi and debutant Naman Dhir among the options. 
But if dew sets in, India’s spinners could find their task considerably harder.
There is also a growing selection subplot in the batting department. The presence of teenage prodigy Vaibhav Sooryavanshi has increased the pressure on 
Sanju Samson
, who has struggled for runs in his last four T20Is, scoring 11, 2, 7 and 9. With the teenager waiting in the wings, another low score could make the competition for the Kerala wicketkeeper-batter’s spot more interesting.
West Indies bowling coach Ravi Rampaul, meanwhile, admitted that his young attack, with most of its members having fewer than 15 or 20 T20I appearances, failed to execute its plans consistently enough.

briefs.headline: Carers uncared for: Lack of regulations make home nurses vulnerable in Keralam
briefs.deck: With changing social patterns, elderly care has become a matter of serious concern for a large number of families in Keralam and hence, support of caregivers has become inevitable. Though in high demand, caregivers often face exploitation. Mithosh Joseph talks to stakeholders to understand their concerns
briefs.bodyText:
For more than two years, Lissy Sunny, a 48-year-old home nurse from Wayanad, has been attending to an elderly woman with dementia.
Lissy stays with the family that hired her to take care of the ageing woman.
From 2019: ‘Most caregivers feel stressed and burdened’
Every morning, after feeding the bedridden woman, Lissy rushes to the kitchen to prepare food for the four-member family with whom she is staying. Her everyday chores end late in the night, long after the family members retire to bed.
All that she is paid for the tiring job is ₹22,000 a month, from which she needs to shell out ₹2,500 as commission to the agent who found her the job.
Geetha Gopi, a home nurse from Alakode in Kannur district, earns less than Lissy and is paid a monthly salary of ₹18,000. She
With the changing social patterns where youngsters are moving out of the State in search of greener pastures and leaving behind their parents at home, elderly care has become a matter of serious concern for a large number of families. The support of caregivers like Lissy and Geetha has thus become inevitable for most of the families to take care of their elders. Even though in high demand, the caregivers are often exploited and underpaid and even denied proper rest. The service of the caregivers often goes unrewarded and unrecognised, complain those in the sector.
“Other than the salary, we are not offered any allowances or incentives for the tedious work we undertake. We work for meagre wages for more than 20 hours a day and that too often without proper rest or reward. Most of the workers have opted for the job due to the financial crisis. Despite the hard work, we are left with no savings. At times, a major portion of the income has to be set apart for medical or travel expenses as we are not covered by any social security schemes,” says Geetha.
The home care agencies that assign work to the caregivers collect service charges from both the families and the home nurses.
“Though the worker would be informed about their monthly salary, they would be kept in the dark about the money the agencies collect from the employer families,” says Sunitha Raja, a home nurse who earlier worked as an agent in a home care agency in Koyilandy in Kozhikode.
Though the agencies offering the service of home nurses are often blamed for the ills plaguing the sector, many people like N. Jose of Wayanad are banking on them to take care of his parents.
“I have been depending on these agencies for obtaining the service of caregivers for more than eight years. Being away from home, it’s not easy for me to find a caregiver in my hometown to take care of my aged parents,” says Jose, who works in London.
However, he adds that some of his friends, who are settled abroad, had unpleasant experiences with unprofessional caregivers and agencies that recruit them.
No employment contracts
In most of the cases, there would not be any legal employment contracts listing out the service conditions of the workers, including the working hours, leave, and overtime wages.
K. Layana, a home nurse from Wadakkancherry in Thrissur who has since left the job, recalls the days when she was forced to attend to the household chores besides her assignment as a caregiver.
“There were occasions when I was asked to do the cooking and cleaning, besides the responsibility as a caregiver to an elderly woman,” she says.
“Most of us cannot afford to question the additional responsibilities forced on us as it may end up in losing the employment,” laments Jayasree, a home nurse.
While there are definite working hours, notified wage structure and well-defined professional responsibilities for the nurses engaged by hospitals and clinics, home nurses and caregivers are left to the mercy of the families engaging them.
“A caregiver constantly needs to be on alert as one does not know when an emergency develops. You are required to provide help when needed,” explains Sangeetha Babu, a home nurse working in Palakkad.
“For a home nurse, weekly off days and leaves do not come naturally but have to be bargained with the family that has engaged them. Such situations would drain the physical and mental health of the caregivers,” says a trained home nurse who works at a care home in Kannur.
“Moreover, it’s not easy to get a replacement for a home nurse who goes on leave for a few days. In some cases, we have to find a substitute caregiver by ourselves to go
Mostly, the caregivers are engaged for 28 days, and availing a day off or leave during the period could lead to loss of wages, complains another home nurse.
The informal nature of the occupation also leaves many caregivers vulnerable to exploitation and denial of basic support in life, including medical insurance or sick leaves, say those in the sector.
“The caregivers lack any social security schemes and even a small health issue could push them to financial distress,” says a 38-year-old home nurse working at Kalpetta in Wayanad.
Many instances of exploitation
A recent workshop organised by the Mahatma Gandhi University in collaboration with the International Institute of Social Studies and the Inter University Centre for Social Science Research and Extension had identified instances of exploitation, insecure working conditions, lack of labour rights and the informal nature of the employment sector as the issues faced by care workers. The conference had called for formalisation of the sector, regulation of private agencies and better wage and training standards.
A policy brief on domestic workers in Keralam by the International Domestic Workers Federation has also noted vulnerabilities including low wages and a lack of work-related social-security benefits. A publication by the Kerala Institute of Labour and Employment had highlighted the issue of leave, health benefits and other protections for domestic and care workers, while calling for government intervention, minimum wages and complaint-redressal mechanisms.
According to experts, the absence of a comprehensive regulatory framework is a matter of concern for both the workers and the families engaging them.
A senior Labour department officer says no focussed study has been undertaken on the living and service conditions of home nurses. According to him, more than 1,000 private agencies, including registered and unregistered, are operating in the State.
In a recent dialogue with the stakeholders, the International Labour Organisation had identified recruitment malpractices, high recruitment costs, under-regulated employment conditions, limited access to grievance redressal and inadequate social protection among the challenges confronting care workers from Keralam.
The Kerala Institute of Labour and Employment had suggested mechanisms such as labour banks or employment centres through local governments as alternatives to complete dependence on private intermediaries.
“Concerns are also being raised about the safety of patients who are left in the care of home nurses as crimes involving caregivers are being reported from different parts of the State. A proposal for mandatory police clearance certificates for home nurses, which was mooted in 2022, is awaiting approval,” says a former police official.
Regulatory framework
There is also demand for introducing regulatory mechanisms for agencies in the sector.
“The agencies should be brought under a management regime where they need to register themselves with the authorities concerned and maintain records related to the services offered by them. There shall be written contracts regarding the salary and other service conditions of caregivers,” suggests K.C. George, who works with a registered charity medical home.
“The agencies provide a common platform for the caregivers and those in need of the services. The firms are not opposed to any regulatory framework planned by the government,” says the proprietor of a home-nursing agency in Kozhikode.
Experts in the health-care sector highlight the need for imparting professional training to the caregivers, which, according to them, would improve the quality of the service besides enhancing their job prospects.
“Caregivers who look after the elderly and bedridden patients need special professional training in safe handling of patients, infection control, nutrition, basic emergency response and the use of care equipment,” suggests Manoj Augustin, a trained nurse in geriatrics, who is currently employed abroad.
The home-based patient care systems and the engagement of caregivers leave much to be desired.

briefs.headline: Fishers from coastal Andhra seek Forest Rights Act-style law to protect fishing grounds
briefs.deck: At a consultation in Visakhapatnam, traditional fishers also ask for early warnings that reach boats at sea and compensation for the closed season
briefs.bodyText:
Traditional fishers from six coastal Andhra districts have asked for a law on the lines of the Forest Rights Act to protect their fishing grounds and access routes from displacement by coastal projects. The demand came at a consultation in Visakhapatnam on Thursday (October 8, 2026) attended by 72 delegates from Konaseema, Kakinada, Anakapalli, Visakhapatnam, Vizianagaram and Srikakulam districts.
The meeting, held at the Fishery Survey of India hall, was organised by the Bay of Bengal Programme Inter-Governmental Organisation (BOBP-IGO), the District Fishermen Youth Welfare Association (DFYWA) and FISHCON. DFYWA executive secretary Arjilli Dasu chaired the sessions. BOBP-IGO representative Ahana Lakshmi and FISHCON president Surada Rajarao took part.
A comprehensive blueprint to safeguard marine small-scale fishers against climate vulnerabilities and tenure insecurity was shaped here on Thursday as 72 traditional fishing delegates from six coastal districts gathered for a high-level consultation workshop.
Hosted at the Fishery Survey of India hall, the event was organised by BOBP-IGO, the District Fishermen Youth Welfare Association (DFYWA), and FISHCON. DFYWA Executive Secretary Arjilli Dasu chaired sessions drawing participants from Konaseema, Kakinada, Anakapalli, Visakhapatnam, Vizianagaram, and Srikakulam districts, alongside BOBP-IGO representative Ahana Lakshmi and FISHCON President Surada Rajarao.
Fishers described how changing weather, storm surges and coastal erosion were shrinking fishing seasons and depleting stocks. They sought district-wise ecological mapping so that ecosystem buffers, safe evacuation routes and storm-proof storage could be built into the State’s disaster plans.
Early warnings at sea
Delegates asked for last-mile early warning systems that deliver multi-day forecasts and wind alerts directly to traditional craft. They recommended linking the alerts with INCOIS ocean forecasts, using NavIC and IoT technologies, and holding community mock drills and running sea ambulances.
Tenure rights
Speakers said ambiguous customary rights left fishers vulnerable to displacement by industry. Delegates urged governments to enact model legislation, on the lines of the Forest Rights Act, to legally safeguard fishing grounds and access corridors**, with** mandatory prior consultation before coastal projects were cleared.
They pointed to jurisdictional overlaps between Central and State authorities within territorial waters, and recommended amending State Marine Fisheries Regulation Acts and Coastal Regulation Zone rules to recognise customary tenure systems and coastal commons.
Participants also sought support for marginalised fishers, particularly women in the value chain: legal awareness programmes, free legal aid clinics in major fishing clusters, non-parametric insurance, structured compensation for mandatory conservation closed seasons and more staff and training for the Fisheries Department.

briefs.headline: Araku Pinery: New experiences at the community-led eco-tourism retreat
briefs.deck: With pottery, camping, adventure rides and seasonal farms joining its pine-lined attractions, Araku Pinery is preparing for a busy tourist season
briefs.bodyText:
The potter’s wheel hums softly beneath the pines. Nearby, birds trade their morning calls as tall trees sway to a breeze carrying a trace of mist. At the wheel, a lump of clay slowly takes shape. Fingers press, steady and sure, as the soft clay turns into a cup, a pot or a small keepsake: a new experience at Araku Pinery.
Pottery is the latest addition to this pine-lined retreat in the Araku Valley. The activity, started recently, gives visitors a chance to sit down, work with clay and take home something they have made themselves.
The timing could not have been better. The tourist season is gathering pace, and the Pinery has been steadily adding experiences to its forest setting. There are camping tents, wooden decks, a tree deck, seasonal gardens and a strawberry patch. Soon, there will be ATV rides and more accommodation options.
The changes are part of a larger experiment in community-led eco-tourism, for which the Andhra Pradesh Forest Department is working with the Van Sanrakshan Samiti of Shanti Nagar village to give an old pine plantation a new purpose.
The additions come at a time when the 27-acre pine plantation is drawing substantially more visitors. Araku Pinery recorded 1.79 lakh visitors during 2025-26. The visitor count marked an 80% rise over the previous year, according to the Andhra Pradesh Forest Department. Revenue during the financial year stood at ₹1.06 crore.
“In the past six months, we have already crossed 65,000 visitors. This October, we are expecting 5,000 visitors per day,” says M Sekhar, manager, Eco Tourism Initiative, Araku Pinery.
The numbers are significant for a location whose revival is closely tied to the local community. Araku Pinery is being managed with the participation of the VSS of Shanti Nagar village. The project records 56 households in the village, with 15 VSS members directly employed at Araku Pinery, a 26-member Dhimsa cultural team and eight members engaged through local shops. In all, 49 families are directly benefited through the activities around the destination.
The Forest Department plans to channel 40% of the revenue generated by the destination towards village development from the next fiscal.
An unusual past
The plantation itself has an unusual history. Tropical pine trees were introduced here in 1975-76 on an experimental basis, making it one of the few such plantations in the Agency areas. The trees grew over the decades, creating the distinctive landscape that visitors now associate with Araku Pinery. Cyclone Hudhud in 2014, however, damaged a substantial portion of the plantation, with around 25% of the pine trees lost.
The Forest Department subsequently took up the revival of the location as an eco-tourism destination. In 2023, an eco-tourism project was inaugurated at an investment of ₹1.06 crore, with support from the Central Warehousing Corporation through its CSR initiative. The project introduced landscaped areas, visitor facilities, decks, camping spaces, a cafeteria and spaces for community activities.
Awards and recognition
The location has now also received State-level recognition for its cleanliness. Araku Pinery was recently presented the Swachha Andhra Award in the Swachha Tourist Place category during the World Tourism Day State government event. Its plastic management measures have become one of the more visible elements of the initiative.
Visitors carrying plastic water bottles need to declare them at the entry point. “Each bottle is labelled and a ₹20 refundable deposit is collected. The bottle has to be returned at the exit to receive the deposit back,” says Sekhar, adding that the Pinery is also encouraging the use of reusable and glass bottles inside the premises.
“The idea is to make people conscious about the waste they bring into a forest landscape. The deposit system also makes visitors responsible for taking the bottle back with them or returning it before they leave,” says Sekhar.
New features
There is more in store for the coming season. Two All Terrain Vehicles (ATV) will be introduced from the second week of October, offering visitors an additional adventure activity. “We also plan to call tenders for the development of mud houses at the spot. Currently, there are 35 tented accommodations that will be available from October 12 onwards,” says Sekhar. There are also plans to add rope and wooden bridges.
Agriculture is being folded into the visitor experience as well. About six acres now wear a carpet of niger plants. Come November and December, the fields are expected to turn a vivid yellow as the flowers bloom, adding a seasonal attraction to the Pinery.
A half-acre strawberry plot is another seasonal attraction. “This is the second year of strawberry cultivation and we are expecting the harvest from November through February,” says Sekhar.
The Pinery already has several spaces designed around slower, Nature-based experiences, including a wooden deck, tree deck, camping area, cafeteria, sunset point and the Ekantaha (solitude) zone. Its setting has also made it a favoured location for photography, pre-wedding shoots and films. The project recorded 1,846 wedding shoots and five film shoots in 2025-26, which brought in another source of revenue to the destination.

briefs.headline: 'Drunk men around me': Assam student's last video from train before she went missing
briefs.deck: Himashri Boro, a 20-year-old student from Assam, was travelling alone after a dance competition. She felt unsafe in her train compartment due to inebriated men surrounding her and reached out to her family. Contact was lost between 2:30am and 3:00am, prompting her family to alert the railway authorities. Her body was later discovered near railway tracks in Andhra Pradesh’s Srikakulam district.
briefs.bodyText:
GUWAHATI: A 20-year-old Assam college student travelling alone on a train after a dance competition had told her family she felt unsafe in a coach surrounded by inebriated men, and had also shared a video of the compartment with a friend, before contact with her was lost in the early hours of October 6.
Her body was found near railway tracks in Andhra Pradesh’s Srikakulam district on Wednesday.
Himashri Boro’s family has alleged murder and accused the Railway Protection Force (
RPF
) of negligence, demanding a thorough investigation into the circumstances leading to her death.
The Northeast Frontier Railway (NFR), however, said the circumstances were under inquiry and that a preliminary probe by the Government Railway Police (GRP) in Palasa prima facie suggested that Boro might have fallen from a moving train.
‘She said she felt unsafe’: Family recounts last call, video
Boro, a resident of Bonda in Assam’s Kamrup Metropolitan district, had travelled to Visakhapatnam with a dance troupe to participate in a competition. She was returning alone ahead of the other members because she had an examination scheduled in Guwahati.
According to her family, she boarded Train No. 22503 at Visakhapatnam around 12.15am on October 6. A local acquaintance, identified by the NFR as Avinash, accompanied her to the station.
CCTV footage showed Boro boarding the train’s S-2 coach with a general ticket, the railway said.
After boarding, she called her sister-in-law and another friend, saying she was uncomfortable with the atmosphere inside the coach.
“After getting on the train, she called me and another friend of hers, and told us that she was feeling uncomfortable in the coach. There were inebriated men all around, making her feel unsafe,” her sister-in-law said.
Boro also shared a video of the coach with a friend, providing a glimpse of the conditions she had described during the call.
Family loses contact between 2.30am and 3am
The family said it lost contact with Boro between 2.30am and 3am and subsequently alerted the railway helpline. They were told that RPF personnel would check on her.
The NFR confirmed that it had received a complaint through the Rail Madad portal on October 6 regarding alleged misbehaviour with a woman passenger aboard the train.
An RPF assistant sub-inspector and other personnel attended to the complaint at Srikakulam Road station. They searched the general and sleeper coaches but could not trace Boro, the railway said.
Her family, however, said it received no subsequent confirmation that she had been located or was safe.
“We never heard back about her being safe. Her body has now been recovered near the railway tracks in Andhra Pradesh. Her two bags have been found intact inside the coach,” her sister-in-law said, calling for a thorough investigation.
Body found between Ponduru and Dusi sections
The RPF later found Boro’s body between the Ponduru and Dusi railway sections in Andhra Pradesh’s Srikakulam district.
The GRP shifted the body to Government RIMS Hospital in Srikakulam for an inquest and autopsy. The circumstances in which she died remain under investigation.
Authorities are recording statements from passengers and the person who accompanied Boro to the station. CCTV footage from Visakhapatnam, Vizianagaram and Srikakulam is also being examined.
The RPF and GRP are coordinating with police in Assam and Andhra Pradesh as the investigation continues.
Assam govt steps in to facilitate return of body
Dimoria MLA Tapan Das said the Assam government would facilitate the return of Boro’s body.
“An autopsy has to be done there. After that, a flight schedule will have to be worked out as there are no direct flights to Guwahati. We are coordinating and trying to ensure that the body can be brought back at the earliest without any family member having to go to claim it,” he said.
The investigation is continuing, with authorities yet to establish the sequence of events that led to Boro’s death.

stories.headline: Friendship, hustle, freedom: The Vixen's Gen-Z playbook
stories.deck: For Bengaluru’s The Vixens Crew, the Gen-Z life isn’t about following a formula. It’s about finding what clicks, taking the risk to pursue it and figuring out the rest along the way
stories.bodyText:
They dance together, work together, celebrate together and have, quite literally, grown up alongside one another. For Bengaluru’s The Vixens Crew, the bond between Medha Naidu, Anushka Anand, Megha J, Bhavana V, Ketaki Vaze and Vibha Vinod Shekhar goes far beyond the dance floor. More than six years of friendship have seen them build a creative life around what they love, figure out how to hustle without burning out, and find their own ways of celebrating. In a candid chat with Bangalore Times, the six friends talk about female friendship, unconventional career paths, finding their own rhythm and why doing things differently comes naturally to them.
The Vixens have known each other for more than six years, so their friendship extends well beyond rehearsals, shoots and social media. “We low-key had the most peak life phases with each other; we almost spent around 8-10 hours together in a day,” says Medha Naidu. That familiarity also shapes how they work. “Each of us brings out different styles. We are learning from each other because each of us is learning different styles every week,” says Medha J.
For Ketaki Vaze, the process is as much about friendship as dance. “Our choreographies are like our way of showing our creativity and for each of us to bond through that creativity,” she says. 
Bhavana V believes being able to disagree without falling out is part of that bond. “Vibha’s opinion can be different, but I can still listen to her point of view and keep my own opinion.” And when one of them needs to vent, the others know that not every problem needs fixing. “I don’t need a solution. If I need a solution, I wouldn’t be coming to you in the first place,” says Megha.
‘We hustle because we found something we connect with’
For the Vixens, the hustle is less about being constantly busy and more about building a life around something they genuinely enjoy. “We hustle so much because we love what we are doing,” says Ketaki. The work is still work, though, they say. “But not too many get the opportunity to do what they love,” says Vibha. “So we are very grateful that it is so amazingly hectic,” she says. Medha adds, “I would choose this hectic over any other. At the end of the day, after dancing and shooting for so long, and I go to my bed, I’m relaxed. I’m like, wow, what a productive day.”
They have also learnt that hustling does not mean pushing through burnout. When things get overwhelming, they pause and reassess. “When that happens, we try to sit together and talk about, okay, what can we do differently? We keep reanalysing that so that we can again refresh our minds and think about things from a different angle,” says Bhavana.
Even their breaks require some planning. "Consistently putting out our content is extremely important to us. So before we take off, we collect a lot of content and put in a lot of hard work, and then take that amazing break where we can rest,” says Megha.
'We are selfish in a good way'
That willingness to build their own path also shapes how the Vixens view careers and success. Vibha explains, “I don’t want to do something that doesn’t give me emotional satisfaction. We are selfish in a good way. For instance, I put myself first. I’ll do something that’s going to bring me happiness, and I’ll figure it out even financially.” Bhavana adds, “Our generation tends to opt to be self-employed over a regular job. For them, choosing a career has less to do with following a prescribed path and more to do with creating their own."
“Society made us believe that nine-to-five jobs were what everyone should take up. I feel things have changed and in our culture, which is quite open to new possibilities, you can do whatever you want. Technology and access to information have also changed the equation. Nobody is forcing us. I think it’s just mentally there for all of us, and we just want to move in that direction,” says Medha, as Anushka adds, “The resources we have now are crazy, and how we’re utilising them is also getting us going.”
‘Female friendship is a sisterhood and a safety net’
For all the talk of hustle and independence, the Vixens’ strongest safety net remains each other. “Female friendship gives you this sort of comfort that probably your family also will not be able to give you sometimes,” says Medha. Bhavana describes it as a “sisterhood” — a space where they can talk about things they may not be able to share elsewhere. That comfort comes from understanding and acceptance, but also from knowing when to simply listen.
‘Every time we shoot, it’s like a festival by itself’
If there is one place where the Vixens’ approach to life comes together, it is in the way they celebrate. For them, festivals mean dressing up, food, family, friends and, naturally, dancing. But tradition is something they engage with on their own terms. “We don’t just follow rituals or culture. We genuinely question things. We only do things that resonate with us or if it makes sense to us,” says Bhavana.
Their celebrations have also become increasingly intertwined with the group. “We have our own festive party before the actual,” says Medha. And sometimes, the work itself becomes a celebration. “Every time we shoot, it’s like a festival itself because we’re all dressed up,” says Anushka.
Perhaps that is what makes The Vixens feel so distinctly of their generation: friendship and work, ambition and fun, tradition and reinvention all exist in the same space.

stories.headline: Cauvery Water Management Authority upholds Cauvery Water Regulation Committee direction to Karnataka to release 3,000 cusecs a day to Tamil Nadu for 15 days
stories.deck: Karnataka had argued that it was reeling under serious hydrological distress which was marked by 54% deficit in cumulative inflows to its four reservoirs in the Cauvery basin
stories.bodyText:
Karnataka, reeling under serious drought, has found itself in a tough situation again with the Cauvery Water Management Authority (CWMA) on Thursday upholding an earlier direction of the Cauvery Water Regulation Committee (CWRC) to the State to ensure release of Cauvery water at a rate of 3,000 cusecs a day for 15 days to Tamil Nadu. The total release for 15 days will add up to 3.88 tmcft.
As per the order, the release will have to commence from 8 a.m. of October 9 (Friday). The stipulated release has to be ensured at Biligundlu inter-State water gauge.
Earlier, Karnataka expressed its inability to ensure any further release on the grounds that it had to prioritise its limited water storage for drinking water requirements. The State pointed out that it was reeling under serious hydrological distress which was marked by 54% deficit in cumulative inflows to its four reservoirs in the Cauvery basin.
As against the 30-year average of 257.633 tmcft inflow, the four reservoirs had received only 257.633 tmcft this season, it said. The State submitted that its water situation was critical as there was no scope for any replenishment since the southwest monsoon, which is the mainstay of its weather system, had ended.
While its reservoirs had a total storage of 46.968 tmcft, the water availability from all sources was estimated to touch 57 tmcft. But the State would need 45 tmcft of water to ensure drinking water supply, environmental flows besides accounting for evaporation, it said, while pointing out that it would be left with a “grossly inadequate” quantum of 12 tmcft for taking care of irrigation needs.
On the contrary, Karnataka argued that Tamil Nadu’s situation was better as it had a storage of 37.997 tmcft in its reservoirs and this was projected to touch 244.997 tmcft considering the downstream contributions and groundwater availability as it was expected to have a normal northeast monsoon.
Karnataka argued that any inter-State water sharing decisions must reflect actual hydrological distress, reservoir storage, intermediate catchment contributions and seasonal rainfall patterns in both the States.
On its part, Tamil Nadu maintained that water release towards irrigating its samba crop had been delayed by 81 days leading to crop stress.
Tamil Nadu maintained that it had received only 46.047 tmcft of water as against the stipulated 127.706 tmcft, leaving a backlog of 15.022 tmcft. It appealed to the CWRC to direct Karnataka to clear this backlog.
After hearing both the States, the CWRC directed Karnataka to ensure the release of 3,000 cusecs a day for 15 days, aggregating to 3.88 tmcft.

stories.headline: 27 to 41: Bengaluru adds 52% more IB schools in five years
stories.bodyText:
Bengaluru:
 Bengaluru recorded a 52% increase in the number of International Baccalaureate (IB) World Schools over the past five years, according to IB data. The city currently has 41 IB World Schools, India’s second-largest concentration after Mumbai, reflecting a steady expansion of the network.
India has 287 IB schools, up from 204 five years ago. Mumbai has 49, followed by Bengaluru with 41, Hyderabad 30, Chennai 18, Gurugram 16 and Pune 14. Delhi and Noida have 8 each. Beyond the largest metropolitan concentrations, Ahmedabad has 7 IB World Schools, Jaipur 6, and Coimbatore and Kochi 5 each.
Demand for IB education is no longer confined to a few major metropolitan markets, said 
Ashish Trivedi
, IB’s head of South Asia and Japan. IB also has a presence in cities including Visakhapatnam and Madurai, with three schools each, as well as Vadodara, Surat, Lucknow, Bhubaneswar, Chandigarh, Kozhikode, Amritsar and Tiruchirappalli.
Karnataka
’s IB network remains concentrated in Bengaluru, with data showing only one authorised IB World School outside the city – in Mysuru. But Trivedi says this could change as awareness and demand expand.
Stating that Bengaluru’s education market has matured, Association of International Schools of India chairperson 
Syed Sultan Ahmed
 said: “Bengaluru parents have access to more information, more choices and greater exposure to different models of schooling. 
That creates an environment where schools experimenting with different curricula and approaches can find an audience.”
Ahmed added: “Bengaluru’s global character is another important factor. For many families, having education that’s internationally recognised and allows children to move between different education systems isn’t simply a preference; it’s a practical consideration.”
KP Gopalkrishna, founder, The International School Bangalore, one of the first IB schools in the city, said: “When Manmohan Singh, as finance minister, opened up the economy and IT sector boomed, many expats returned. But they couldn’t find a matching school for their children when they returned. So we started a school with world class facilities.”
Sarojini Rao, principal, Indus International School, said: “When we started 25 years ago, there was a market for IB schools as IGCSE was the only other international curriculum offered. What attracted parents that time, and mostly even now, is that IB is considered a passport to foreign universities. We’re trying to make parents aware that it’s much more than that. We opted for IB for the flexibility it allows. It permits us to empower students with competencies and innovation so they can charter their future.”
Experts said one reason for concentration in Bengaluru is the lack of an ecosystem in rural areas. Sultan said shortages of teachers and school leaders trained to teach differently affected the quality and costs. As more schools adopted international curricula, the main challenge would be ensuring enough well-trained teachers and capable school leaders to deliver the education envisaged by such curricula.
Sanjay Palsamudram, CEO, 7Rays Semiconductors, said, “I had chosen IB because I realised it provides holistic education and critical thinking away from rote learning. It also introduces the concept of research at an early stage. After two daughters having graduated from IB schools, am happy at how it has shaped them in their outlook, perspectives and decisions.”

briefs.headline: Citizens take on GBA West chief over Kanteerava Studio Road in Bengaluru
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru: Citizens openly confronted Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA) West City commissioner KV Rajendra on the condition of Kanteerava Studio Road on Wednesday. A video of the face-off during a road inspection on Wednesday has gone viral.
The war of words came days after a massive crater opened up on the already-damaged stretch between Surana College and Nandini Layout following heavy rain. The road surface appeared to have caved in along one edge of the carriageway, leaving behind a deep, water-filled cavity.
The video shows Vivek C, vice-president of Yuva Ghataka Bengaluru Urban and a regular commuter on the stretch, speaking to the commissioner during an inspection of the road.
Vivek told 
TOI he chance-met Rajendra and sought clarity on the timeline of pending repairs. “He told me he has been here only for a year. But that cannot be an excuse,” Vivek said. The commissioner allegedly responded in a very rude manner when he enquired about delay in fixing the road. “Aren’t these officials here to serve the public? Don’t we have the right to question them?” he said.
Rajendra defended his actions and said while citizens’ frustration was justified, their behaviour during the confrontation was not. “I do take full responsibility and I’ll take action against one of our assistant executive engineers for failure in duty. But that does not give anyone the right to behave in such a manner, shout at officials or fall on moving vehicles,” Rajendra told 
TOI
.
The commissioner said he had personally inspected the road soon after taking charge of the zone last year, but the stretch had already been earmarked for white-topping, limiting the scope for major interim repairs. “Because the road was kept for white-topping, we could not do much. I was inspecting the stretch again and assessing what best could be done when this incident took place. We will take up work on Kanteerava Studio Road within the next two days, subject to weather conditions,” he said.
Rajendra claimed West Zone office had not received any formal complaints regarding the road’s condition, a point disputed by local commuters who insist that they have repeatedly raised the issue with various authorities.
However, Vivek said, “The stretch has been in a terrible condition for years. Neither the corporation nor MLAs or MPs have managed to permanently fix it. The latest crater was just the tipping point. No matter how many times people raise their voice, authorities remain quiet. Such roads are taking lives and putting hundreds of commuters in danger every day. This cannot be accepted.”

briefs.headline: CMRS completes Pink Line safety inspection in Bengaluru
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru: Commissioner of Metro railway safety (CMRS), southern circle, Thursday completed the three-day statutory safety inspection of Metro’s 7.5-km elevated Pink Line between Kalena Agrahara and Tavarekere.
BMRCL said V Venkatasubramanian and team conducted a motor trolley inspection of the main line and associated infrastructure Tuesday. The next day, they checked Kothanur depot facilities and conducted train trials, testing and another motor trolley inspection. The operations control centre at Byappanahalli was inspected Thursday.
BMRCL had obtained a speed certificate from Research Designs and Standards Organisation in Aug 2026 and railway board subsequently granted provisional sanction for rolling stock, while the independent safety assessor certified the signalling system.
CMRS inspection is a statutory safety assessment required before authorisation to open the section for public service. CMRS will issue authorisation subject to compliance with observations and conditions stipulated during the inspection.
Once the elevated Pink Line opens, Metro’s operational network will expand from 96.1km to 103.6km. The corridor will improve connectivity along Bannerghatta Road and adjoining areas and strengthen Bengaluru’s public transport network.
The elevated section has six stations: Kalena Agrahara, Hulimavu, IIMB, JP Nagar 4th Phase, Jayadeva Hospital and Tavarekere.

briefs.headline: Duo hid smuggled gold biscuits under baggage trolleys, caught at Bengaluru airport
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru:
 An attempt by two passengers to conceal gold packets under baggage trolleys was foiled by Directorate of Revenue Intelligence (DRI) at Kempegowda International Airport Wednesday, with officials seizing 12 biscuits worth nearly Rs 1.8 crore.
DRI Bengaluru zonal unit officials placed the two passengers arriving from Kuala Lumpur under surveillance. The two were seen attaching packets containing gold under trolleys before walking away from them.
According to DRI, the plan was to avoid carrying the smuggled gold through customs. Instead, the packets were deliberately left concealed beneath the trolleys, which would subsequently be used by unsuspecting passengers to carry their luggage.
The two passengers monitored the movement of trolleys and passengers using them. Investigators suspect their intention was to allow the trolleys to cross the customs-controlled area before retrieving the concealed gold. However, DRI officers intercepted the operation and recovered 12 gold biscuits in two packets.

stories.headline: Two Mumbai-based firms, five Indian nationals face U.S. sanctions over Iran oil trade
stories.deck: The action against the Indian entities and individuals is part of the U.S. crackdown against Iran under Operation Economic Outcast
stories.bodyText:
The U.S. on Thursday (October 8, 2026) imposed sanctions on two Mumbai-based firms and five Indian nationals associated with them over allegations of being involved in the trade of petroleum products from Iran.
The U.S. Department of State action targeted SSPL Solutions Private Limited and Samudra Marine Services Private Limited for facilitating the import of petroleum products from Iran.
Two persons associated with SSPL Solutions — Dhwani and Nisarg Vora, and three persons related to Samudra Marine Services — Ketan Kochikar, Bhupendrasingh Sahu and Harishyam Hariharan Chundakattil have also been blocked from performing any transactions related to their respective firms.
The action against the Indian entities and individuals is part of the U.S. crackdown against Iran under Operation Economic Outcast.
“The Department of State is sanctioning ten entities, six individuals, and five vessels in connection with trade in Iranian-origin petroleum, petroleum products, and petrochemical products,” an official statement said.
The State Department said these entities channelled millions of dollars to the Iranian regime, bolstering one of its most critical revenue streams and enabling its continued illicit conduct.

stories.headline: Oil prices today: Brent slips as Trump cites 'productive talks' with Iran
stories.bodyText:
Oil prices fell on Friday as concerns over Middle East supply disruptions eased after US President 
Donald Trump
 said Washington would not attack Iran before next month's US elections. He also cited progress in talks aimed at ending the conflict, which has disrupted global oil markets.
Brent crude futures fell 72 cents, or 0.7%, to $103.53 a barrel, while US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude futures declined 52 cents, or 0.6%, to $90.97 by 7:50 am IST.
Despite Friday's decline, Brent was on track for a weekly gain after settling 4% higher on Thursday amid increased attacks earlier this week on vessels carrying crude oil out of the Middle East.
WTI, however, was set for a slight weekly decline despite supply disruptions caused by a hurricane approaching the US Gulf Coast.
Earlier on Thursday, Trump said Washington was having “productive discussions” with Iran and that no attack was planned before the November 3 US midterm congressional elections. His remarks came after media reports suggested he was considering military action before the polls.
Iran's Tasnim news agency reported that foreign minister Abbas Araqchi said Tehran was reviewing Washington's response to its proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days.
The US continues to apply economic pressure on Iran in an effort to end the conflict, which is now in its eighth month.
On Thursday, Washington imposed fresh sanctions targeting individuals, networks and 17 vessels allegedly involved in transporting Iranian crude oil, petroleum products and petrochemicals.
Oil prices have fluctuated this week amid growing threats to shipping in the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz. Before the war, the strategic waterway handled shipments equivalent to about 20% of global oil and fuel supplies.
Oil markets are also monitoring Hurricane Isaias in the Gulf of Mexico. The storm has forced producers to shut in about 1.3 million barrels per day, or 62.9% of current oil production in the region, as of Thursday, according to the US Marine Minerals Administration.
Oil markets have remained unsettled for more than seven months since the conflict in the Middle East began. Despite the latest gains, prices remain below the $126-a-barrel level reached earlier in the crisis.

stories.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: After IndiGo, Air India, Air India Express and Akasa have also hiked fuel surcharge due to spiralling price of aviation turbine fuel (ATF/jet fuel) and falling rupee, which is acting as a double whammy at a time when air traffic is also beginning to decline as higher fares are seeing price-sensitive domestic travellers shift to other modes of transport.
Flying will get even more expensive this festive season. Air India group's new distance-based surcharge for domestic flights now ranges between Rs 400 (upto 500 km) and Rs 1,200 (over 2,000 km). The surcharge on international flights now ranges between $55 (West Asia) and $215 (North America).
"The latest increase in fuel prices has further elevated operating costs for airlines, with fuel continuing to account for a substantial proportion of overall airline expenditure," Air India said in a statement. Akasa's earlier fuel surcharge was in the range of Rs 199 and Rs 1,300. This range will now be between Rs 375 and Rs 2,500.

stories.headline: Gold, silver imports by banks, nominated agencies to attract 3% IGST
stories.deck: This is done to ensure parity of taxes imposed on gold and other precious metal imports through other routes, including bullion
stories.bodyText:
Gold, silver and platinum imports by banks and nominated agencies attract 3 per cent IGST effective April 1, 2026, Revenue Secretary Arvind Shrivastava said on Thursday (October 8, 2026).
The Government notified the GST Council on Thursday (October 8, 2026) that the list of designated banks and agencies that attract IGST exemptions on gold and precious metal imports has not been extended beyond March 31, 2026, Shrivastava said.
This is done to ensure parity of taxes imposed on gold and other precious metal imports through other routes, including bullion.
Gold, silver and platinum imports attract a 3% IGST, but before April 1, 2026, the tax was exempt when the precious metals were imported by banks and nominated agencies – a list of which is notified by the Government periodically.
That list was not notified on April 1 this year as gold, silver and precious metal imports, which led to forex outgo, became a concern for the Government. India is the world's second-biggest gold consumer after China and gold imports are driven by the jewellery industry demand.
In May, the government had also hiked import duty on gold and silver to 15%, from 6%, and on platinum to 15.4%, from 6.4%, to curb non-essential imports.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi too has given a clarion call to avoid gold purchases, amid stress on the rupee following a rise in import bills after the Iran-US-Israel war.
Gold imports during April-August 2026-27 grew by 3.38% to $17.47 billion, while silver imports declined 8.81% to $1.74 billion.
